t: Mint: Cost-Efficient Tracing with All Requests Collection via Commonality and Variability Analysis
pb: Distributed tracing systems face a fundamental tension between preserving essential trace information and reducing the massive volume of traces generated in production. The prevailing '1 or 0' binary sampling strategy either retains a full trace or discards it entirely, which fails to efficiently capture structural commonality across traces while still recording meaningful variability.
me: Mint decomposes traces into a commonality skeleton shared across structurally similar requests and per-request variability deltas that capture deviations. It collects all requests but stores only the variability delta relative to the common template, reducing storage volume while preserving full per-request observability. A commonality and variability analysis pass extracts templates offline or incrementally from the trace stream.
nv: Replacing binary trace sampling with a commonality-variability decomposition that retains full-request coverage at drastically reduced storage cost.
th: All-requests distributed tracing via commonality-variability decomposition

t: EXIST: Enabling Extremely Efficient Intra-Service Tracing Observability in Datacenters
pb: Intra-service application-level tracing imposes 5-10% average runtime overhead on traced applications (up to 18% worst case), making it impractical for continuous deployment in shared, stressed datacenters where sub-percent-level overhead is required for practical observability.
me: EXIST redesigns the intra-service tracing pipeline to achieve per-mille-level overhead through a combination of: extremely lightweight instrumentation hooks that avoid expensive context-switching or synchronization, asynchronous off-path trace collection and encoding that decouples tracing cost from the critical path, and selective event compression that preserves causality chains while discarding redundant intermediate events. The specific mechanism targets eliminating redundant data copies and reducing synchronization in the trace record path.
nv: A holistic intra-service tracing system redesigned from instrumentation to collection to achieve per-mille-level overhead, roughly 10-50x lower than existing schemes, while maintaining full causal observability.

mx.other: overhead reduced from 5-10% (up to 18% worst case) to per-mille level

th: Ultra-low-overhead intra-service tracing for datacenters

t: TempGraph: An Efficient Chain-driven Temporal Graph Computing Framework on the GPU
pb: Temporal graph path problems require vertices to be processed sequentially along time-dependent chains, creating inherently poor parallelism and slow convergence that prevents existing GPU solutions from utilizing the massive thread-level parallelism and high memory bandwidth of modern GPUs.
me: TempGraph transforms the temporal graph into disjoint time-dependent chains that expose temporal dependencies explicitly, then employs a Generate-Activate-Compute (GAC) execution model to decouple temporal dependencies between different chains by maintaining a set of shortcut references. This allows multiple chains to be processed concurrently by massive GPU thread pools while shortcut maintenance handles cross-chain dependency resolution, enabling fast convergence and high parallelism.
nv: The Generate-Activate-Compute model with inter-chain shortcut references that breaks temporal dependencies across disjoint chains, enabling concurrent GPU execution of temporally-coupled graph workloads.

mx.speedup: 3.0-16.2x over GPU baselines; 33.9-368.9x over TeGraph CPU baseline

th: GPU temporal graph execution via chain decomposition and GAC model

t: Cascade: A Dependency-aware Efficient Training Framework for Temporal Graph Neural Network
pb: TGNN training is severely constrained by temporal dependencies between input events: large batches improve parallelism but cause infrequent node memory updates leading to stale information and accuracy degradation, forcing small-batch training with high latency and underutilized hardware.
me: Cascade uses a topology-aware scheduler that packs as many spatially-independent events as possible into the same batch, then leverages inter-node memory similarity to identify 'stabilized' nodes whose memories have converged sufficiently to safely break temporal dependencies. This similarity-based dependency breaking allows temporally-independent events to be included in larger batches. An adaptive update frequency mechanism based on runtime feedback further reduces redundant memory updates, achieving 2.3x average (up to 5.1x) speedup without accuracy loss.
nv: Similarity-based temporal dependency breaking that identifies stabilized nodes whose memory states can be safely treated as independent, enabling large-batch TGNN training without sacrificing accuracy.

mx.speedup: 2.3x average, up to 5.1x over prior TGNN training frameworks

th: Dependency-aware large-batch training for temporal graph neural networks

t: Extended User Interrupts (xUI): Fast and Flexible Notification without Polling
pb: Intel's existing User Interrupt (UIPI) mechanism for fast user-space notification has correctness and performance limitations that prevent it from matching shared-memory polling latency while maintaining the efficiency of asynchronous notification. Current designs lack support for preemption in user-level runtimes, kernel-bypass timers, and efficient interrupt forwarding to accelerators.
me: xUI extends Intel's UIPI model with four hardware mechanisms: (1) tracked interrupts that allow senders to know when an interrupt was delivered, (2) hardware safepoints that let user-level runtimes implement preemption without kernel involvement, (3) a kernel-bypass timer for deadline-driven scheduling, and (4) interrupt forwarding to route notifications directly to accelerators (modeled on Intel's DSA). The design is modeled and evaluated in gem5 full-system simulation, measuring end-to-end latency for three distinct use cases.
nv: Hardware safepoints that enable user-level runtime preemption without kernel involvement, combined with interrupt forwarding to accelerators, all built on an extended user-interrupt model.

mx.other: performance of shared-memory polling with efficiency of asynchronous notification

th: hardware extensions for fast user-space interrupt notification without polling

t: AnA: An Attentive Autonomous Driving System
pb: Current autonomous driving perception modules execute unconditionally and uniformly regardless of driving context, wasting compute on irrelevant scenes and missing safety-critical events that require focused attention—a mismatch from how humans selectively allocate perception resources.
me: AnA refactors the ADS perception-planning interface with three mechanisms: (1) a query interface that lets the planning module express interest in specific perceptual targets using driving knowledge; (2) a query executor that maps these queries to an optimal subset of active perception tasks; and (3) a monitor that uses driving knowledge to detect and handle anomalous task executions. The system distinguishes between ambient awareness (broad, low-cost perception) and focused attention (targeted, high-fidelity perception on safety-critical elements), dynamically switching modes based on planner queries.
nv: A query-driven perception architecture that couples planning knowledge to selective activation of perception tasks, enabling human-like attentive driving that reduces compute by 44% while halving collisions on adversarial benchmarks.

mx.speedup: 44% compute reduction without compromising driving safety
mx.other: 2x reduction in collisions on adversarial events

th: Query-driven attentive perception scheduling for autonomous driving

t: Energy-aware Scheduling and Input Buffer Overflow Prevention for Energy-harvesting Systems
pb: Energy-harvesting IoT devices capture data at a fixed rate but process it at a dynamically varying rate determined by available ambient power; when capture rate exceeds processing rate the fixed-size input buffer overflows and events are permanently lost, and no existing dynamic solution prevents this across varying energy and workload conditions.
me: Quetzal combines a hardware power-measurement circuit with a two-part software runtime. The energy-aware scheduler selects jobs by minimizing end-to-end latency including projected energy recharging time, not just execution time. The runtime uses queueing-theory models to predict whether the selected job will cause an input buffer overflow before it completes; if overflow is imminent, it degrades the scheduled job (e.g., reduces quality or shortens duration) to lower processing latency and prevent buffer saturation. The hardware circuit is simple and system-agnostic, providing real-time power readings to the scheduler.
nv: Integration of queueing-theory-based IBO prediction with energy-recharge-aware scheduling and job degradation, enabled by a lightweight hardware power measurement circuit, to dynamically prevent input buffer overflow on energy-harvesting devices.

mx.other: Up to 4.2x reduction in events missed due to input buffer overflow vs. baselines

th: Energy-aware scheduling with IBO prevention for energy-harvesting IoT devices

t: Past-Future Scheduler for LLM Serving under SLA Guarantees
pb: LLM serving frameworks using continuous batching suffer from either overestimation of memory consumption (conservative schedulers) or underestimation leading to harmful request evictions (aggressive schedulers), because neither accurately accounts for the dynamic memory release profile of concurrently running requests across future decoding steps.
me: The Past-Future scheduler combines two components: (1) output length distribution prediction that samples predicted output lengths from the empirical distribution of recent historical requests (a sliding window of ~1,000 finished requests), updating each running request's predicted remaining length at every decode step using the conditional distribution P(l > l_current); and (2) future required memory estimation that sorts running requests by estimated remaining length, computes memory occupancy at each future completion event, and determines peak future memory as max(M_t+1, M_t+2, ...) across all future completion times. A queued request is admitted only if adding it keeps peak future memory below hardware capacity. This is implemented in LightLLM with <1% scheduling overhead using GPU-parallel computation.
nv: The observation that LLM output length distributions are stable within adjacent time windows enables a parameter-free, model-agnostic historical-distribution sampling approach to precisely estimate peak future KV-cache memory demand for the entire running batch, eliminating both conservative underutilization and aggressive eviction.

mx.speedup: 2-3x higher goodput over aggressive/conservative schedulers under heavy load
mx.other: Memory utilization approaches theoretical optimum (93-94% vs 98% oracle) while eviction rate drops to ~3-7% vs 93% for aggressive at watermark=99%; 50-60% throughput improvement on multimodal LLaVA and Qwen-VL models

th: history-aware future memory estimation for LLM serving scheduler goodput

t: Exo 2: Growing a Scheduling Language
pb: User-schedulable languages (USLs) fix a single design point for what programmers control and what is automated, but no universal control/automation split exists even in narrow domains, causing USLs to be inextensible when new hardware targets or optimization strategies emerge.
me: Exo 2 enables users to define new scheduling operations externally to the compiler by composing a set of trusted fine-grained primitives (actions for modifying code, inspection for querying code structure, and references for pointing to code locations). The key mechanism is Cursors, a new abstraction that unifies code references across actions, inspections, and scheduling library composition, allowing safe user-defined scheduling transformations. Users build scheduling libraries that amortize transformation effort across related kernels without modifying the compiler internals.
nv: The Cursor abstraction that enables users to write fully externalized, composable scheduling libraries safe from compiler internals, allowing the scheduling language to grow without core modifications.

mx.speedup: Performance competitive with state-of-the-art on 3 platforms
mx.other: Scheduling code reduced by ~10x across 80+ kernels

th: extensible user-schedulable compiler language

t: Accelerating LLM Serving for Multi-turn Dialogues with Efficient Resource Management
pb: Current LLM serving frameworks recompute attention keys and values for all prior turns on each new query in a multi-turn dialogue, incurring substantial redundant compute overhead. Additionally, the long accumulated prompt lengths from multi-turn context cause head-of-line blocking under FCFS scheduling, underutilizing GPU resources.
me: The paper introduces efficient resource management for multi-turn LLM serving by preserving KV-cache state across turns to eliminate recomputation of prior-turn attention keys and values. A new scheduling policy replaces FCFS with a length-aware or priority-based scheduler that avoids head-of-line blocking by reordering or preempting long-prompt requests. KV-cache memory is managed dynamically to balance cache retention across concurrent multi-turn sessions, trading off memory capacity against recompute cost.
nv: Cross-turn KV-cache retention combined with a head-of-line blocking-aware scheduler specifically designed for the multi-turn dialogue serving regime.

mx.other: GPU utilization improvement and latency reduction for multi-turn dialogues (details in full paper)

th: multi-turn KV-cache management and scheduling for LLM serving

t: Forecasting GPU Performance for Deep Learning Training and Inference
pb: Predicting GPU performance for deep learning workloads on unseen GPU models (new GPU on existing model, or existing model on new GPU) is inaccurate with prior ML-based approaches, which attempt to predict end-to-end kernel latency directly and suffer >100% error on new model-GPU pairs.
me: NeuSight decomposes a single DL kernel prediction into smaller working sets called 'tiles' that correspond to the GPU's SM-level execution granularity. Tile-granularity predictions are made by a learned ML model, then aggregated across tiles to estimate end-to-end latency. The approach is bounded by fundamental performance laws (roofline model) and incorporates both GPU hardware parameters and software library optimizations (cuDNN, cuBLAS heuristics) to constrain the prediction space, enabling generalization to unseen GPUs by parameterizing hardware characteristics rather than encoding GPU identity.
nv: Decomposing DL kernel latency prediction to tile granularity aligned with SM execution, bounding predictions via performance laws, enabling accurate cross-GPU generalization without running code on the target hardware.

mx.accuracy: GPT-3 inference latency error reduced from 30.8% (SOTA) to 2.3% on H100; training error reduced from 121.4% to 2.3%
mx.other: evaluated across diverse DL workloads and up-to-date GPUs including H100

th: tile-level ML-based GPU performance forecasting for unseen hardware

t: Concurrency-Informed Orchestration for Serverless Functions
pb: Serverless FaaS platforms suffer excessive cold starts because existing container keep-alive policies ignore concurrent invocations: they fail to reason about whether reusing a busy container (delayed warm start) or cold-starting a new container is preferable, and they make imbalanced eviction decisions that prematurely evict soon-to-be-reused containers.
me: CIDRE is a container orchestration algorithm that combines fine-grained container-level state (busy/idle, time-to-free) with coarse-grained concurrency signals to speculatively decide between a delayed warm start and a cold start under concurrent scaling. For eviction, CIDRE uses both container-level recency and concurrency-aware reuse probability to produce balanced eviction decisions that avoid removing containers still likely to be reused. The algorithm is evaluated on two production FaaS workload traces.
nv: CIDRE is the first FaaS keep-alive policy to explicitly model container concurrency state and use it to make speculative warm-vs-cold-start decisions and balanced eviction choices simultaneously.

mx.speedup: up to 39.3% average invocation overhead reduction
mx.other: up to 75.1% cold start ratio reduction vs state-of-the-art keep-alive policies

th: Concurrency-aware serverless container orchestration

t: lambda-trim: Optimizing Function Initialization in Serverless Applications With Cost-driven Debloating
pb: In serverless FaaS platforms, Function Initialization (package import, module loading) accounts for more than 50% of the monetary cost of cold starts in real-world ML applications, yet existing optimization efforts focus on the container/VM startup phase rather than the Python initialization phase.
me: lambda-trim uses a three-stage automated pipeline: a static analyzer identifies the reachable module dependency graph for a given serverless function, a profiler specialized for the serverless pricing model (which accounts for both memory usage and wall-clock time as billing dimensions) quantifies the latency and cost contribution of each module, and a debloater removes redundant code paths and unused modules while preserving correctness. The optimized application is directly deployable on standard serverless platforms without runtime changes.
nv: Serverless-pricing-model-aware profiling that jointly optimizes for latency and memory (both billing dimensions) to prioritize debloating decisions, specifically targeting the Function Initialization phase.

mx.speedup: substantial reductions in cold-start latency (not quantified in abstract)
mx.other: Function Initialization >50% of monetary cold-start cost in real-world ML applications

th: Cost-driven Python debloating for serverless function initialization

t: Embracing Imbalance: Dynamic Load Shifting among Microservice Containers in Shared Clusters
pb: Containers within the same microservice deployed in large shared clusters experience temporal and spatial performance imbalance due to resource contention; standard load-balancing policies assume homogeneous container performance and respond with over-provisioning, wasting resources while still frequently violating SLAs.
me: The paper proposes dynamic load shifting, a system that continuously monitors per-container performance metrics (latency, throughput) to detect imbalance and dynamically steers incoming requests toward higher-performing containers within the same microservice. Rather than treating imbalance as a problem to eliminate through uniform scheduling, the system embraces it by exploiting performance heterogeneity: hot containers receive fewer requests and cool containers receive more, allowing the cluster to extract more useful work without additional provisioning. The approach integrates with existing cluster schedulers and load balancers.
nv: Treating intra-microservice container performance imbalance as an exploitable signal for dynamic load shifting rather than a scheduling defect to eliminate.

mx.other: substantial resource wastage reduction vs over-provisioning approach (not quantified in abstract)

th: Imbalance-aware dynamic load shifting for microservice containers

t: Dilu: Enabling GPU Resourcing-on-Demand for Serverless DL Serving via Introspective Elasticity
pb: Serverless DL serving systems use coarse-grained static GPU allocation that produces 15-94% GPU fragmentation due to dynamic workload patterns; existing horizontal-only scaling cannot adapt GPU resource allocation fine-grainedly within a running DL function instance, degrading utilization and violating QoS.
me: Dilu introduces Introspective Elasticity (IE), a two-dimensional co-scaling mechanism combining vertical scaling (adjusting GPU resource allocation within a running DL task) and horizontal scaling (adding/removing instances). Dilu uses multi-factor profiling with efficient pruning search to characterize each DL function's GPU compute/memory sensitivity. A cross-layer scheduler applies resourcing-complementary principles to fill fragmented GPU capacity with compatible DL tasks. At runtime, an adaptive 2D co-scaling controller continuously monitors QoS signals and adjusts both per-instance GPU allocation and the number of instances to minimize fragmentation while meeting SLAs.
nv: Introspective Elasticity (IE) enables live two-dimensional (vertical + horizontal) GPU resource adjustment for serverless DL functions without full restarts, eliminating the coarse-grained static allocation that creates GPU fragmentation.

mx.speedup: up to 1.8x inference throughput; 1.1x training throughput improvement
mx.other: 10-46% GPU defragmentation; 11-71% QoS violation rate reduction vs SOTA baselines

th: Two-dimensional GPU elasticity for serverless DL serving

t: Helix: Serving Large Language Models over Heterogeneous GPUs and Network via Max-Flow
pb: Serving LLMs across heterogeneous GPU clusters (differing GPU types, memory capacities, and interconnect speeds) is inefficient because existing systems cannot jointly optimize model placement and request scheduling to account for both GPU and network heterogeneity simultaneously.
me: Helix models the LLM inference computation over a heterogeneous cluster as a max-flow problem on a directed, weighted graph where nodes represent GPU instances and edge capacities encode both GPU compute throughput and network bandwidth. A Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solver operates on this graph to jointly discover optimized model placement (which layers/shards go where) and request scheduling (how tokens are routed through the cluster), treating the two tasks as a unified optimization rather than solving them independently.
nv: Formulating heterogeneous LLM serving as a max-flow problem that jointly optimizes model placement and request scheduling in a single MILP, exposing trade-offs invisible to decoupled approaches.

mx.speedup: up to 3.3x throughput over existing approaches
mx.other: prompting latency reduced up to 66%, decoding latency reduced up to 24%

th: Max-flow-based joint model placement and scheduling for heterogeneous LLM serving

t: vAttention: Dynamic Memory Management for Serving LLMs without PagedAttention
pb: PagedAttention enables dynamic KV cache allocation during LLM inference by breaking virtual memory contiguity, but this non-contiguous virtual memory layout for KV caches introduces non-trivial programming complexity and performance overheads in attention kernels and memory management logic. The changes to virtual memory layout require rewriting attention kernels and force suboptimal memory access patterns.
me: vAttention leverages OS virtual memory primitives (specifically, demand paging and virtual address space reservation) to provide contiguous virtual address spaces for KV caches while still allowing on-demand physical memory allocation. Instead of managing non-contiguous page tables in user space as PagedAttention does, vAttention reserves large contiguous virtual address ranges for KV caches upfront and relies on the OS to back them with physical pages on demand. This preserves contiguous virtual memory semantics seen by attention kernels, enabling use of standard (unmodified) CUDA attention kernels while still preventing physical memory fragmentation.
nv: Achieving dynamic KV cache memory allocation with a contiguous virtual address layout by exploiting OS demand-paging, eliminating the need for custom non-contiguous memory management in attention kernels.

mx.other: throughput improvement over vLLM (PagedAttention); specific numbers not in abstract

th: OS-based contiguous virtual memory for LLM KV cache management

t: PICACHU: Plug-In CGRA Handling Upcoming Nonlinear Operations in LLMs
pb: Nonlinear operations in LLMs (e.g., softmax, layer norm, GELU, RoPE) contribute significantly to inference latency and are poorly served by fixed-function accelerators designed primarily for matrix multiply/convolution, as they require user-defined precision and flexible dataflow to handle diverse operator shapes and precision requirements.
me: PICACHU uses a Coarse-Grained Reconfigurable Array (CGRA) as a plug-in accelerator specifically targeting nonlinear operations in LLMs. The CGRA is configured with reconfigurable processing elements (PEs) arranged in a spatial dataflow grid that can be reprogrammed per operator, supporting user-defined precision via configurable compute units. PICACHU plugs into existing accelerator pipelines (e.g., alongside a systolic array or GPU) and offloads nonlinear operations while the main compute handles linear algebra. The CGRA dataflow is scheduled at compile time per operator using a mapping tool that assigns CGRA PE configurations and routing to match the operator's precision and shape requirements.
nv: A plug-in CGRA accelerator specifically co-designed with LLM nonlinear operation diversity, providing reconfigurable PE-level precision and dataflow to handle softmax, layer norm, GELU, and similar operations that fixed-function units cannot efficiently support.

mx.other: latency reduction for nonlinear ops; specific numbers not in abstract

th: CGRA plug-in accelerator for LLM nonlinear operations

t: TaOPT: Tool-Agnostic Optimization of Parallelized Automated Mobile UI Testing
pb: Parallelizing automated mobile UI testing across multiple test devices is inefficient because existing tools explore overlapping UI subspaces on different devices, wasting resources by redundantly testing similar app states. No existing approach optimizes the parallelization of arbitrary automated UI testing tools without modifying their internal workflow.
me: TaOPT performs online UI subspace inference by analyzing the App Under Test (AUT) to identify loosely coupled UI subspaces—regions of the app's state graph that can be explored independently. TaOPT then coordinates access to these subspaces across different testing devices, guiding each device's testing tool toward distinct, unexplored subspaces without modifying the tool's internal search logic (tool-agnostic). This subspace partitioning and assignment is updated dynamically as testing progresses, using observations of which subspaces each device has covered to avoid redundancy. By separating exploration across devices at the subspace granularity, TaOPT maximizes coverage diversity.
nv: Online inference of loosely coupled UI subspaces and tool-agnostic cross-device subspace assignment that prevents redundant exploration without requiring modifications to the underlying testing tool.

mx.speedup: 60% less testing duration for comparable code coverage
mx.other: 1.2-2.1x more unique crashes detected under same resource budget

th: tool-agnostic parallel UI test optimization via subspace partitioning

t: Coach: Exploiting Temporal Patterns for All-Resource Oversubscription in Cloud Platforms
pb: Cloud platforms remain significantly underutilized across all resource types (CPU, memory, network, storage) because existing oversubscription approaches target only a single resource (typically CPU), causing the oversubscribed bottleneck to shift to other resources and leaving overall utilization low. Memory oversubscription is especially difficult because memory is non-fungible — physical pages cannot be quickly reassigned between VMs.
me: Coach introduces CoachVM, a general-purpose VM type that partitions each resource into a guaranteed portion (always allocated, PA-backed for memory) and an oversubscribed portion (allocated on demand from a shared pool, VA-backed for memory using zNUMA to deprioritize cold pages via guest NUMA policy). A prediction model (random forest regressor) predicts per-VM resource utilization in time windows (e.g., 3x8-hour daily windows) using VM configuration, weekday, subscription history, and customer-specific features, computing per-resource oversubscription rates per time window. The cluster scheduler uses these per-time-window predictions to colocate VMs with complementary temporal patterns, maximizing multiplexing savings. A per-server oversubscription agent monitors resource utilization and applies reactive mitigations (local resource reassignment) or proactive mitigations (VM migration) to prevent SLO violations when contention occurs.
nv: Holistic all-resource oversubscription of cloud VMs using temporal utilization pattern prediction to colocate complementary workloads, with a PA/VA memory partition (zNUMA) that enables transparent memory oversubscription for unmodified guest VMs.

mx.other: ~26% more VMs hosted per server with minimal performance degradation; 4x6hr time windows save ~15% memory and ~20% CPU vs single-lifetime-max allocation

th: temporal pattern-based holistic cloud VM resource oversubscription

t: RESCQ: Realtime Scheduling for Continuous Angle Quantum Error Correction Architectures
pb: Continuous angle quantum error correction architectures require non-deterministic resource state production, meaning statically generated schedules waste cycles when states fail and must be re-attempted. Without a realtime scheduler, execution time is unnecessarily long and classical control overhead for frequent rescheduling can dominate.
me: RESCQ is a realtime scheduler for continuous angle QEC architectures that actively redistributes resources on-demand based on expected production rates of rotation states. It monitors resource state generation success and, upon failure, dynamically reassigns resources from lower-priority to higher-priority operations to minimize total cycle count. To control classical control overhead, RESCQ adaptively selects the recomputation frequency based on the state of the system, reducing unnecessary scheduling invocations when the system is stable.
nv: Dynamic, on-demand redistribution of quantum resources in continuous angle QEC systems with adaptive recomputation frequency to balance cycle-count minimization against classical control overhead.

mx.speedup: average 2x improvement in cycle count over baseline static proposals

th: realtime scheduling for quantum error correction resource management

t: TAPAS: Thermal- and Power-Aware Scheduling for LLM Inference in Cloud Platforms
pb: LLM inference workloads exhibit fine-grained millisecond-scale phase transitions (prefill vs. decode) with distinct thermal and power profiles, which traditional cloud thermal and power management techniques are too coarse-grained to handle effectively. Cloud co-location of SaaS and IaaS workloads with differing visibility levels further complicates scheduling.
me: TAPAS is a thermal- and power-aware scheduler for LLM inference that models the per-phase (prefill/decode) thermal and power profiles of inference workloads at millisecond granularity. It leverages LLM configuration parameters (model parallelism, model size, quantization level) as scheduling knobs to trade off performance, temperature, power consumption, and output quality. The scheduler accounts for co-located SaaS and IaaS workloads, applying different control strategies depending on the level of visibility and flexibility available for each workload type.
nv: A scheduler that explicitly models the millisecond-scale thermal and power phase transitions of LLM inference and uses quantization, parallelism, and model size as scheduling knobs to jointly optimize thermal, power, and performance objectives in a multi-tenant cloud.

mx.other: specific headline numbers not provided in abstract

th: thermal- and power-aware scheduling for LLM inference in cloud datacenters

t: CoServe: Efficient Collaboration-of-Experts (CoE) Model Inference with Limited Memory
pb: Collaboration-of-Experts (CoE) inference on memory-constrained edge devices (e.g., RTX 3080Ti with 12 GB GPU memory) requires serving hundreds of expert models (e.g., 300+ ResNet101/YOLOv5 experts totaling 60 GB) that cannot fit in GPU memory, forcing expert swapping from CPU or SSD where switching latency accounts for over 90% of total inference latency.
me: CoServe exploits expert dependency, a key property of CoE inference where the routing module determines expert sequences offline (unlike MoE where routing is runtime-only). Three mechanisms are combined: (1) dependency-aware request scheduling that groups requests using the same expert together within a queue window and assigns requests to minimize total inference time across parallel CPU+GPU executors; (2) dependency-aware expert management with a two-stage eviction policy that first evicts dependency-orphaned subsequent experts (sorted by memory footprint) and then evicts by ascending usage probability (computed offline from routing rules); (3) an offline profiler using microbenchmarks to determine optimal memory allocation (via a CDF-based sliding decay window search over expert count) and executor configuration per device.
nv: Exploiting the deterministic routing structure of CoE (pre-assessable expert usage probabilities and dependency graphs) to enable dependency-aware request scheduling and expert eviction that is impossible in MoE systems where routing is only known at runtime.

mx.speedup: 4.5x to 12x throughput over Samba-CoE on NUMA and UMA devices
mx.other: expert switching reduced by up to 93.87% (1060 to 65 switches); expert switching latency is 90%+ of total inference latency in baseline

th: Dependency-aware scheduling and memory management for CoE model serving

t: Towards End-to-End Optimization of LLM-based Applications with Ayo
pb: LLM-based applications consist of both LLM and non-LLM components whose combined end-to-end latency is not jointly optimized by existing frameworks, which use coarse-grained task-module orchestration that confines optimizations within individual modules.
me: Ayo introduces a fine-grained, end-to-end workflow optimizer for LLM-based applications that breaks down application pipelines below the task-module boundary, enabling cross-module scheduling decisions. The system models the full application DAG and applies joint optimization of LLM inference scheduling alongside non-LLM compute stages to minimize overall pipeline latency.
nv: Cross-module, end-to-end scheduling that jointly optimizes LLM and non-LLM pipeline stages rather than treating them as isolated task modules.

mx.other: end-to-end latency reduction (specific numbers not in abstract)

th: End-to-end LLM application workflow optimization

t: FlexSP: Accelerating Large Language Model Training via Flexible Sequence Parallelism
pb: Existing sequence parallelism methods for long-context LLM training assume homogeneous (equal-length) sequences and apply a single static scattering strategy, causing severe load imbalance when real training corpora have heterogeneous, long-tail sequence length distributions.
me: FlexSP introduces flexible sequence parallelism that adapts the scattering strategy per-sequence to match each sequence's actual length. The system dynamically selects the degree of sequence parallelism and the scattering pattern (e.g., how many devices a sequence is split across) based on the length distribution of the current batch, balancing workload across devices and reducing idle time from length imbalance. Communication and attention computation are co-optimized under the flexible strategy.
nv: Per-sequence adaptive scattering in sequence parallelism that dynamically matches parallelism degree to each input sequence's length, addressing the load imbalance caused by heterogeneous sequence lengths.

mx.other: improved training throughput over static sequence parallelism (specific numbers not in abstract)

th: Flexible sequence parallelism for heterogeneous-length LLM training

t: Spindle: Efficient Distributed Training of Multi-Task Large Models via Wavefront Scheduling
pb: Training multi-task, multi-modal (MT MM) foundation models is inefficient because their heterogeneous model components and diverse workloads across tasks and modalities create complex dependency patterns that existing parallelism strategies cannot jointly optimize. No existing distributed training system addresses the combined challenges of workload heterogeneity and dependency-driven execution scheduling for MT MM models.
me: Spindle decomposes MT MM model execution into 'waves'—groups of heterogeneous micro-tasks—and applies a two-phase joint optimization: (1) heterogeneity-aware workload parallelization that assigns tasks to devices accounting for differing compute demands per modality, and (2) dependency-driven wavefront scheduling that pipelines waves based on their inter-task data dependencies. The wavefront schedule coordinates execution so that waves from different tasks and modalities overlap in time, filling pipeline bubbles caused by load imbalance.
nv: The wavefront scheduling abstraction that decomposes MT MM model execution into heterogeneous waves and jointly optimizes parallelization and dependency-driven scheduling in a single framework.

mx.speedup: up to 71% over state-of-the-art training systems

th: heterogeneity-aware distributed training scheduling

t: Using Analytical Performance/Power Model and Fine-Grained DVFS to Enhance AI Accelerator Energy Efficiency
pb: DVFS on AI processors has historically been applied at coarse granularity (entire program or sub-phases) because the control latency of DVFS mechanisms exceeds the duration of individual AI operators, leaving per-operator energy optimization unexploited. This coarse-grained DVFS fails to match voltage/frequency to the actual compute intensity of each AI operator.
me: The paper proposes an analytical performance/power model that characterizes the compute- and memory-boundedness of individual AI operators, enabling prediction of which operators tolerate voltage/frequency reduction without performance loss. Combined with a hardware mechanism to reduce DVFS control latency, the system applies fine-grained DVFS at the AI-operator level: memory-bound operators run at lower frequency while compute-bound operators run at peak frequency, minimizing energy waste during memory-stall phases.
nv: Operator-level DVFS control for AI accelerators enabled by an analytical performance/power model that predicts the energy-latency trade-off per operator without runtime profiling.

mx.energy_or_tops_w: energy efficiency improvement (specific numbers not in abstract)

th: fine-grained DVFS for AI accelerator energy efficiency

t: D-VSync: Decoupled Rendering and Displaying for Smartphone Graphics
pb: The VSync-based rendering architecture on smartphones tightly couples the rendering pipeline to the display refresh cycle, causing frame drops and increased rendering latency when large high-frame-rate screens and complex visual effects (physics-based animations, stunning UI) demand rendering time that exceeds the VSync interval. This rigid coupling prevents flexible scheduling of rendering work across display periods.
me: D-VSync decouples the rendering pipeline from the display refresh cycle by separating the rendering scheduler from the VSync signal, allowing rendering to be completed asynchronously relative to display timing. t: Medusa: Accelerating Serverless LLM Inference with Materialization

t: ChameleonEC: Exploiting Tunability of Erasure Coding for Low-Interference Repair

t: The Importance of Generalizability in Machine Learning for Systems

t: VR-Pipe: Streamlining Hardware Graphics Pipeline for Volume Rendering

t: Adyna: Accelerating Dynamic Neural Networks with Adaptive Scheduling

me: Adyna uses a unified representation to model diverse DynNN variants and introduces a dynamism-aware multi-kernel selection paradigm. At runtime, a dataflow scheduler observes the distribution of dynamic size values (e.g., number of active tokens or blocks) and selects among multiple precompiled kernels, each optimized for a specific dynamic-size bucket. An effective kernel sampling algorithm chooses the minimal set of kernels to precompile and cache on the accelerator, balancing coverage against on-chip memory cost. The hardware architecture supports multi-tile and multi-tenant execution to handle concurrent dynamic workloads.

t: Make LLM Inference Affordable to Everyone: Augmenting GPU Memory with NDP-DIMM
pb: Deploying large LLMs (e.g., LLaMA2-70B) on consumer-grade GPUs with limited VRAM is impractical; offloading model weights to host DRAM or NVMe storage creates severe bandwidth bottlenecks on the PCIe interconnect, resulting in very low inference throughput.
me: Hermes partitions LLM weights into 'hot' neurons (~20% of parameters, ~80% of compute) and 'cold' neurons (~80% of parameters, ~20% of compute) based on activation sparsity. Hot neurons are mapped to the consumer GPU for compute-efficient execution, while cold neurons are offloaded to near-data processing (NDP) units embedded in commodity DRAM DIMMs. A lightweight runtime predictor dynamically classifies neurons as hot or cold based on input activations. A window-based online scheduler maintains load balance across multiple NDP-DIMM modules, enabling pipelined heterogeneous execution between GPU and NDP-DIMMs.

t: Mascot: Predicting Memory Dependencies and Opportunities for Speculative Memory Bypassing
pb: Memory dependence prediction (MDP) and speculative memory bypassing (SMB) require conflicting predictor properties: MDP tolerates false positives but not false negatives, while SMB tolerates false negatives but not false positives. Prior TAGE-based predictors for either mechanism fail to learn patterns of non-dependence, causing inaccuracy.
me: Mascot is a TAGE-inspired predictor that learns both dependence and non-dependence contexts. Unlike prior designs that only learn dependence patterns, Mascot tracks the history of non-aliasing outcomes in the TAGE table entries, enabling low false negative rates required for MDP and low false positive rates required for SMB from a single shared structure. The predictor is used in two modes: MDP-only (for load issue gating) and combined MDP+SMB (for value forwarding from store to load bypassing address resolution).
nv: A unified TAGE-based predictor that explicitly learns non-dependence patterns, enabling both memory dependence prediction and speculative memory bypassing with a single compact hardware structure.

t: ARTEMIS: Agile Discovery of Efficient Real-Time Systems-on-Chips in the Heterogeneous Era

me: ARTEMIS integrates a dynamic SoC-level scheduler into the DSE loop to eliminate the mapping dimension from the search space, dramatically pruning the effective design space. The scheduler incorporates policies such as task procrastination and memory-traffic/energy-aware task assignment. DSE heuristics use real-time deadline-aware and power/area-aware ranking mechanisms to guide the remaining architecture search. The method is validated on FPGA hardware and evaluated on autonomous vehicle and AR/VR application suites.

t: InstAttention: In-Storage Attention Offloading for Cost-Effective Long-Context LLM Inference

A flash-aware in-storage attention engine executes the attention decode phase directly inside the CSD, with KV cache management mechanisms tailored to flash access patterns (e.g., large sequential reads). Optimized P2P transmission between GPU and CSDs eliminates unnecessary data migration back across PCIe. The system targets offline inference of a 13B model on an NVIDIA A6000 GPU.

t: HILP: Accounting for Workload-Level Parallelism in System-on-Chip Design Space Exploration
pb: Early-stage heterogeneous SoC design space exploration tools (MultiAmdahl, Gables) only model minimum and maximum workload-level parallelism (WLP) extremes; they cannot model realistic mixed-application workloads where multiple independent multi-phase applications share an SoC's heterogeneous cores and accelerators.
me: HILP formulates SoC workload scheduling as a job-shop scheduling problem: a set of independent multi-phase applications with phase-level dependencies is to be scheduled across heterogeneous cores and accelerators. This is solved using an integer linear programming (ILP) solver to find a near-optimal schedule that minimizes total workload execution time subject to power and memory bandwidth constraints. The ILP captures the full continuum of WLP (not just extremes) and can be used to sweep large design spaces efficiently during early exploration.
nv: Modeling heterogeneous SoC workload scheduling as a job-shop scheduling ILP, enabling early-stage design space exploration that captures the full spectrum of workload-level parallelism rather than just min/max extremes.

t: DynamoLLM: Designing LLM Inference Clusters for Performance and Energy Efficiency
pb: LLM inference clusters running on GPU-dense infrastructure consume excessive energy and incur high operational carbon emissions because existing systems provision resources for peak load at maximum GPU frequency and tensor parallelism, ignoring the strong heterogeneity in request types (input/output length variation) and diurnal load fluctuations that create large energy-saving opportunities.
me: DynamoLLM is a hierarchical three-level energy management framework (Cluster Manager, Pool Manager, Instance Manager) that dynamically reconfigures a GPU cluster across three knobs: number of inference server instances (scale in/out), tensor parallelism (shard up/down), and GPU frequency (scale up/down). The cluster is partitioned into per-request-type instance pools (classified by input/output token length into SS/SM/.../LL buckets); a BERT-based output-length predictor routes requests to the appropriate pool. Configuration selection is formulated as a MILP optimization using offline energy-performance profiles, with a hierarchical approximation heuristic for real-time operation. Reconfiguration overheads are minimized by: pre-warming VMs from snapshots, direct NVLink weight re-sharding via a bipartite graph matching algorithm (minimizing weight transfers), and keeping nvidia-smi loaded in-memory for rapid GPU frequency changes.
nv: A hierarchical multi-knob (instance count + tensor parallelism + GPU frequency) dynamic reconfiguration framework for LLM inference clusters that maintains per-request-type resource pools and minimizes reconfiguration overheads via weight-stationary NVLink re-sharding and proactive VM pre-warming.

t: Lincoln: Real-Time 50~100B LLM Inference on Consumer Devices with LPDDR-Interfaced, Compute-Enabled Flash Memory
pb: Consumer devices cannot run large 50-100B LLM models in real time because: (1) Flash storage has insufficient internal read bandwidth for per-iteration weight loading, and (2) the conventional Flash interface (NVMe/UFS) offers far lower transmission bandwidth to the NPU than DRAM interfaces, making both the prefill and decode phases severely bandwidth-limited.
me: Lincoln is a device-architecture co-design with two complementary solutions for the two LLM phases. For the compute-intensive prefill phase, Flash devices use the existing high-speed LPDDR interface (normally used for DRAM) to transmit weights to the NPU at much higher bandwidth than conventional Flash interfaces, while maintaining cost/area efficiency. For the memory-intensive decode phase, hybrid-bonding-based near-Flash computing performs matrix-vector operations directly on Flash dies to exploit the full internal Flash bandwidth without transmission bottlenecks, coupled with speculative decoding to further reduce latency. On the device level, Flash internal bandwidth is increased by improving array shrinking methods (lower read latency, more parallel Flash planes per die), leveraging 3D hybrid bonding already in consumer Flash products.
nv: Phase-specific dual strategy: using the LPDDR high-speed interface for prefill-phase weight streaming from Flash, and hybrid-bonding near-Flash compute for decode-phase GEMV execution directly on Flash dies.

t: CogSys: Efficient and Scalable Neurosymbolic Cognition System via Algorithm-Hardware Co-Design

t: LAD: Efficient Accelerator for Generative Inference of LLM with Locality Aware Decoding
pb: In LLM autoregressive decoding, the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length, and at lengths beyond 2048 tokens the attention mechanism's repeated read of the full KV cache becomes the dominant bottleneck, consuming over 50% of total inference time on GPU-based systems.
me: LAD (Locality Aware Decoding) is a dedicated ASIC accelerator that exploits numerical locality in attention scores across consecutive decoding steps. The key insight is that when an attention score at a specific sequence position remains approximately constant across several consecutive decoding steps, the corresponding key and value vectors need not be re-fetched at every step. LAD implements a locality detection engine that identifies stable-score positions and caches their contribution, dramatically reducing KV cache access frequency while maintaining decoding accuracy. The hardware includes specialized attention decoding units paired with on-chip score history buffers to track and exploit inter-step score locality.

t: BOSS: Blocking algorithm for optimizing shuttling scheduling in Ion Trap

pb: Single Flux Quantum (SFQ) circuits face area overhead from path balancing and pipelining, compromising scalability despite high performance potential.
me: Timing-aware framework inspired by CMOS EDA jointly optimizes clock phase assignments, pipelining, and splitter tree construction. Explicitly models gate delays and operates polynomial-time algorithms for scalability.

t: Enabling Decoder-only Language Model Inference on a CNN Accelerator
pb: CNN accelerators cannot efficiently run decoder-only language models due to non-computational operations in attention (head merging/splitting, transpositions), lack of floating-point support for Softmax and RMSNorm, and memory-bound operations during generation that degrade throughput.

pb: Mobile LLM inference constrained by limited memory bandwidth and compute. Speculative inference increases compute-intensive GEMM operations creating new trade-offs for GEMV-accelerated PIM. Redundant draft tokens waste energy.

t: H3D-LLM: Heterogeneous 3D Chiplet Design for LLM Inference with Dynamic Task Scheduling and Memory-Aware Orchestration
pb: 3D chiplet integration for LLM inference faces three critical challenges: asymmetric compression constraints from sparsity-precision tradeoffs, tier-level load imbalance from static resource allocation, and coupling-induced signal degradation in high-density TSV networks.

t: EarDVFS: Environment-Adaptable RL-based DVFS for Mobile Devices
pb: Conventional DVFS methods struggle with mobile device demands including device-specific thermal calibrations, ambient environment impact, and non-processor component thermal effects.
me: EarDVFS: environment-adaptable RL-based DVFS with proactive throttling, tracking of ambient and non-processor temperatures, environment-robust RL parameter design, and device-specific configuration awareness.

t: BIGX - GPU-accelerated dynamic programming for buffer insertion (timing violations)
pb: Buffer insertion for timing violation recovery involves solving a large dynamic programming problem to determine optimal buffer placement on signal nets. Traditional CPU-based approaches are computationally expensive and slow.
me: BIGX implements Van Ginneken's buffer insertion algorithm on GPU using parallelized dynamic programming, distributing the subproblem computation across GPU threads and optimizing memory access patterns for GPU architecture.

t: MASIM - multi-array scheduler for SIMD logic-in-memory to reduce copy instructions
pb: SIMD logic-in-memory (LIM) systems require frequent data copying between memory and processing arrays, creating bottlenecks. Scheduling across multiple arrays to minimize data movement is a complex optimization problem.
me: MASIM provides a multi-array scheduling framework that orchestrates computation across multiple SIMD processing arrays while minimizing data copy operations through intelligent task assignment and data placement strategies.
nv: Multi-array scheduling approach for SIMD logic-in-memory systems that explicitly optimizes for reducing copy instruction overhead.
th: Multi-array memory-compute scheduling

t: Twill: Scheduling Compound AI Systems on Heterogeneous Mobile Edge Platforms
pb: Compound AI systems chain multiple models (DNNs, transformers, LLMs) on mobile edge platforms with dynamic workloads and heterogeneous computational demands, challenging existing scheduling methods.
me: Run-time framework using task affinity-aware cluster mapping, priority-aware task freezing/unfreezing, and Dynamic Voltage/Frequency Scaling (DVFS) to minimize latency within power budgets.
nv: First run-time framework for scheduling concurrent DNN-transformer-LLM inference on heterogeneous mobile edge platforms.
th: Run-time scheduling for compound AI systems on mobile platforms

t: AMALI: An Analytical Model for Accurately Modeling LLM Inference on Modern GPUs
pb: Existing GPU analytical models cannot accurately predict LLM inference performance because they mismodel tensor core throughput, ignore constant and instruction cache effects, and abstract away warp-level execution details critical to LLM kernels.
me: AMALI introduces three modeling innovations: (1) an instruction-modifier and throughput-based tensor core model that captures math-pipe throttle stalls by accurately modeling the pipeline fill/drain behavior of tensor cores; (2) micro-benchmark-derived analytical models for constant cache and instruction cache that measure CUDA kernel launching latencies; (3) a multi-warp model using warp instruction number distributions to reflect the heterogeneous occupancy and scheduling behavior of LLM inference kernels. All three components are validated against real A100 hardware measurements.
nv: The explicit modeling of instruction-cache and constant-cache latencies via micro-benchmarks, combined with a throttle-stall-aware tensor core model, reduces LLM inference MAPE from 127.56% to 23% on A100.

mx.accuracy: MAPE reduced from 127.56% to 23% on A100

th: analytical GPU performance modeling for LLM inference

t: GCStack+GCScaler: Fast and Accurate GPU Performance Analyses Using Fine-Grained Stall Cycle Accounting and Interval Analysis
pb: Existing GPU performance analysis tools use coarse-grained, issue-stage-centric, priority-based cycle stacks that exaggerate memory-side stalls, hide concurrent stall events, and require expensive cycle-level simulation repetition for each design variant.
me: GCStack captures all concurrently occurring stall events within each cycle and represents performance as a fine-grained cycle stack by attributing each stall cycle to all simultaneously active stall types rather than the single highest-priority one. GCScaler then uses interval analysis to analytically scale the fine-grained cycle stack from a baseline GPU to an alternative design point without re-simulation, applying separate analytical scaling models for idle and synchronization stalls. The combined method allows exploration of 1,000 GPU designs from a single simulation trace.
nv: Fine-grained concurrent stall accounting (GCStack) combined with interval-analysis-based analytical stall scaling (GCScaler) enables simultaneous accurate bottleneck attribution and fast design-space exploration from a single baseline simulation.

mx.speedup: 32.7x faster design exploration over repetitive timing simulation
mx.accuracy: 6.37% mean absolute performance estimation error across 47 benchmarks

th: fast and accurate GPU performance analysis and design-space exploration

t: WindServe: Efficient Phase-Disaggregated LLM Serving with Stream-based Dynamic Scheduling
pb: Phase-disaggregated LLM serving systems that separate compute-bound prefill from memory-bandwidth-bound decoding still suffer from coarse-grained static scheduling that leaves prefill compute overloaded while decoding resources sit idle, creating queuing delays and underutilization. KV cache transfers between disaggregated phases introduce additional scheduling overhead that further degrades latency SLOs.
me: WindServe implements a global scheduler that continuously monitors compute and memory resource usage across prefill and decoding pools and dynamically orchestrates cross-phase job assignments to reduce queuing delay and KV-cache swapping overhead. A stall-free rescheduling strategy saturates memory resources while minimizing overhead from KV cache transfers between phases. A stream-based pipeline mitigates interference between prefill and decoding jobs running concurrently by separating their execution streams and managing dependencies asynchronously.
nv: WindServe's stall-free rescheduling strategy enables continuous saturation of memory resources during KV cache migration between disaggregated phases without introducing scheduling stalls, enabling fine-grained dynamic load balancing that static schedules cannot achieve.

mx.speedup: 4.28x TTFT median improvement; 1.5x TPOT P99 reduction vs SOTA phase-disaggregated systems
mx.other: improved SLO attainment under high load

th: dynamic scheduling for phase-disaggregated LLM inference serving

t: Fair-CO2: Fair Attribution for Cloud Carbon Emissions
pb: Existing cloud carbon attribution methods unfairly allocate operational and embodied carbon footprints to tenant workloads by ignoring dynamic demand effects on embodied carbon amortization and interference effects in colocated scenarios. This leads to mispriced carbon signals that fail to incentivize workload-level carbon optimization.
me: Fair-CO2 adopts the Shapley value from cooperative game theory as a theoretically fair ground truth for shared-cost attribution, capturing both dynamic demand effects on embodied carbon (hardware amortized proportionally to actual utilization, not flat time allocation) and interference effects from workload colocation. Because exact Shapley computation scales exponentially with the number of workloads, Fair-CO2 approximates it via two tractable components: demand-aware embodied carbon attribution (adjusting hardware depreciation by real-time utilization) and interference-aware resource cost attribution (accounting for performance degradation from co-tenancy). Monte Carlo simulations over workload schedules and colocation scenarios are used to validate the approximation's fidelity to the exact Shapley solution.
nv: Applying the Shapley value as a principled fairness criterion for cloud carbon attribution and introducing scalable approximations that decompose it into demand-aware embodied and interference-aware operational components.

mx.accuracy: Monte Carlo simulations show Fair-CO2 approximates Shapley ground truth attribution at scale
mx.other: Fair attribution of operational and embodied carbon in colocated cloud scenarios

th: fair game-theoretic carbon footprint attribution for cloud workloads

t: Dadu-Corki: Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Embodied AI-powered Robotic Manipulation
pb: Embodied AI robotic manipulation systems run LLM inference on a frame-by-frame basis, creating cumulative sequential latencies (LLM inference, robot control, data communication) that reach 249 ms per frame and prevent real-time operation at >=30 Hz. LLM inference alone consumes 72.7% of latency and 95.8% of energy per frame.
me: Corki decouples LLM inference from robot control by replacing per-frame discrete action prediction with cubic polynomial trajectory prediction over multiple future steps, reducing LLM inference frequency by up to 5.1x. A custom dataflow ASIC accelerator implements task-space computed torque control (TS-CTC) with pipelined link-level computations (pose, velocity, acceleration, force units connected via FIFOs and line buffers) and an application-specific approximate computing unit that skips matrix recomputation when joint angular movement is below a threshold (saving >51% of matrix updates). Communication latency is hidden by pipelining image capture and transmission concurrent with trajectory execution.
nv: Replacing frame-by-frame discrete action prediction with cubic trajectory prediction decouples the LLM inference rate from the control rate, enabling a purpose-built TS-CTC hardware accelerator with approximate computing that achieves 29x control speedup on FPGA.

mx.speedup: 5.9x end-to-end; 29x control acceleration on FPGA; LLM inference frequency reduced 5.1x
mx.area: 13.6% DSP, 7.8% FF, 16.9% LUT, 6.6% BRAM on Xilinx Zynq-7000 ZC706
mx.accuracy: Success rate improvement up to 13.9% (up to 17.3% average job length improvement on seen tasks)

th: Algorithm-architecture co-design for real-time LLM-controlled robotic manipulation

t: RAGO: Systematic Performance Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Serving
pb: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) serving is emerging as a critical LLM deployment pattern, but diverse RAG algorithm variants exhibit wildly different workload characteristics (retrieval latency, reranking compute, generation length), making a single optimization strategy inadequate. There is no systematic framework for characterizing and optimizing across the space of RAG pipelines.
me: RAGO introduces RAGSchema, a structured abstraction encoding the components and dataflow of any RAG algorithm, used to characterize and compare workload behaviors. The paper analyzes representative RAG variants with distinct schemas, exposing performance bottlenecks. RAGO then applies algorithm-specific system optimizations—scheduling policies, resource partitioning, and batching strategies—tuned to each RAGSchema's profile, rather than treating all RAG variants uniformly as extended LLM inference workloads.
nv: RAGSchema is the first structured abstraction that captures the full diversity of RAG algorithm variants, enabling principled, schema-driven performance optimization rather than ad-hoc per-system tuning.

mx.speedup: 2x QPS per chip vs. RAG-extended LLM serving systems
mx.other: 55% reduction in time-to-first-token latency

th: schema-driven optimization for RAG serving systems

t: AiF: Accelerating On-Device LLM Inference Using In-Flash Processing
pb: On-device LLM inference with SSD offloading is severely bottlenecked by the limited external read bandwidth of flash storage (NAND-to-host path), making inference latency unacceptably high even though LLM weight matrices fit in flash capacity. Existing SSD offloading engines are bound by PCIe/interface bandwidth rather than the high internal NAND bandwidth.
me: AiF integrates matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) compute units directly inside flash chips (Accelerator-in-Flash), exploiting the high internal NAND plane-level bandwidth without routing data across the external interface. Two novel flash read techniques are introduced specifically for LLM weight access patterns stored in flash memory. AiF also employs a streamlined error correction process that delivers a 4x boost in internal read bandwidth with minimal overhead, enabling in-flash GEMV operations to run at near-full internal bandwidth.
nv: AiF is the first in-flash processing design that embeds GEMV computation within flash chips and introduces flash-read techniques tailored to LLM weight layout, achieving 4x internal bandwidth amplification through a lightweight ECC scheme.

mx.speedup: 14.6x throughput over SSD offloading baseline; 1.4x over in-memory inference
mx.other: 4x boost in internal flash read bandwidth during inference

th: In-flash GEMV acceleration for on-device LLM inference

t: H2-LLM: Hardware-Dataflow Co-Exploration for Heterogeneous Hybrid-Bonding-based Low-Batch LLM Inference
pb: Edge-side low-batch LLM inference (personal assistant, reception bot, private edge server) is bottlenecked by the DRAM bandwidth wall: existing NMP designs embed compute engines inside DRAM dies, limiting compute capacity and creating an imbalance between bandwidth and computation for both prefill (compute-bound) and decoding (bandwidth-bound) stages. Hybrid-bonding technology offers a path to higher compute capacity near memory, but the trade-off between computation capacity and bandwidth has not been systematically explored.
me: H2-LLM proposes a hybrid-bonding-based heterogeneous accelerator that places high-capacity compute dies in face-to-face contact with DRAM dies, exploiting the high through-silicon-via bandwidth of hybrid bonding. The architecture exposes a design space covering compute tile counts, memory bandwidth allocation, and die partitioning. A data-centric dataflow abstraction is introduced to map LLM operations (attention, feed-forward, KV-cache access) onto the heterogeneous on-die and near-die compute resources across both prefill and decoding stages. A design space exploration (DSE) framework automatically searches this joint architecture-dataflow space for the Pareto-optimal configuration.
nv: H2-LLM is the first system to jointly explore the hardware architecture and dataflow design space for hybrid-bonding-based heterogeneous LLM accelerators, using a data-centric dataflow abstraction that maximally exploits the heterogeneous compute and bandwidth resources.

mx.speedup: 2.72x geomean over in-die NMP-based heterogeneous accelerators
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 1.48x geomean better energy efficiency vs in-die NMP baseline

th: Hybrid-bonding heterogeneous architecture and dataflow co-exploration for edge LLM inference

t: Hybe: GPU-NPU Hybrid System for Efficient LLM Inference with Million-Token Context Window
pb: LLM inference with million-token context windows is infeasible on GPUs alone because KV cache activation memory for long contexts (>100K tokens) exceeds total GPU DRAM capacity, making batching impractical and leaving GPU compute cores severely underutilized during the memory-bandwidth-bound decode stage. The compute-memory imbalance between compute-intensive prefill and memory-intensive decode cannot be addressed by batching when KV data dominates physical memory.
me: Hybe assigns the compute-intensive prefill stage to existing high-throughput GPUs (NVIDIA H100 with vLLM) and offloads the memory-bandwidth-bound decode stage to lightweight NPUs sized with exactly enough compute to saturate their HBM bandwidth. The key mechanism is fine-grained KV transmission: as the GPU produces partial KV activations during prefill, it immediately streams them to NPU HBM over interconnect, reducing peak GPU memory footprint dramatically. A stage-wise pipeline scheduler dynamically assigns incoming requests to idle GPU or NPU hardware, minimizing pipeline stalls across the two-stage heterogeneous system. Hybe NPU is implemented in 4nm process with HBM matching the H100 HBM specification.
nv: Fine-grained KV streaming that incrementally offloads partial KV tensors from GPU to NPU during prefill, enabling million-token context windows without GPU memory overflow while keeping NPUs minimally provisioned for decode-stage bandwidth saturation.

mx.speedup: 2.1x for Phi-3 with 100K-token context vs H100 GPU
mx.energy_or_tops_w: 3.9x energy efficiency for Llama-3 with 1M-token context vs equal-count H100 GPUs

th: Heterogeneous GPU-NPU disaggregation for long-context LLM inference

t: Hermes: Algorithm-System Co-design for Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation At-Scale
pb: As RAG datastores expand into the trillions of tokens, the retrieval phase dominates end-to-end latency and energy, undermining the benefits of using RAG to augment LLM outputs. Existing RAG systems lack mechanisms for efficiently routing queries to relevant subsets of a distributed datastore at scale.
me: Hermes partitions the RAG datastore across multiple nodes and uses a hierarchical search strategy that dynamically routes queries to relevant datastore subsets. A coarse-grained index tier rapidly identifies high-relevance partitions, and only those partitions are subjected to full dense retrieval (exact k-NN or approximate ANN). This co-design eliminates unnecessary retrieval computation on irrelevant partitions while maintaining retrieval quality.
nv: Hermes combines datastore partitioning with intelligent hierarchical query routing that adapts to query-to-partition relevance, reducing retrieval compute without sacrificing recall.

mx.speedup: 9.33x end-to-end latency reduction vs. state-of-the-art for trillion-token RAG
mx.accuracy: No sacrifice in retrieval quality

th: Distributed hierarchical retrieval for trillion-token RAG

t: HardHarvest: Hardware-Supported Core Harvesting for Microservices
pb: Software core harvesting—where batch 'Harvest VMs' temporarily steal idle cores from latency-critical 'Primary VMs'—incurs prohibitive overheads (hypervisor calls, TLB/cache flushes, context switches) that are acceptable for monolithic applications but intolerable for sub-millisecond microservices.
me: HardHarvest implements core harvesting entirely in hardware by adding in-hardware request scheduling logic that detects idle cores in Primary VMs and assigns them to Harvest VM tasks without hypervisor intervention. TLBs and caches are partitioned between Primary and Harvest VMs using a smart replacement algorithm that protects Primary VM working sets, enabling rapid context transfer without full TLB/cache flushes. The hardware scheduler monitors Primary VM request queues and preempts Harvest VM work before Primary VM tail latency is impacted.
nv: HardHarvest is the first hardware architecture for core harvesting in microservice environments, eliminating software overheads by combining in-hardware request scheduling with TLB/cache partitioning and a smart replacement policy.

mx.speedup: 1.8x Harvest VM throughput; 6.0x Primary VM tail latency reduction vs. software core harvesting
mx.other: 1.5x core utilization improvement

th: Hardware-supported core harvesting for microservice tail latency

t: GPUs All Grown-Up: Fully Device-Driven SpMV Using GPU Work Graphs
pb: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) on GPUs requires expensive host-side preprocessing to select per-row algorithms based on non-zero distribution, forcing costly CPU-GPU round-trips and limiting cache locality. This preprocessing adds latency that is particularly problematic for iterative solvers with repeated SpMV calls.
me: The paper leverages GPU Work Graphs, a novel GPU programming model originally designed for graphics, to implement fully device-driven SpMV self-scheduling. Work Graphs enable fine-grained dataflow execution of individual workgroups using emerging GPU hardware and firmware support (AMD GPUs with rocSPARSE stack). Preprocessing is fused with per-row computation: as soon as preprocessing generates sufficient work metadata, workgroups of specialized per-row SpMV kernels are self-scheduled and dispatched on-device without host interaction. This interleaving improves L1/L2 cache locality and eliminates CPU-GPU synchronization entirely. The approach uses a fixed 25 MiB device-side supporting data structure independent of matrix size, contrasting with scaling structures in rocSPARSE LRB.
nv: Applying GPU Work Graphs—a hardware/firmware-level on-device self-scheduling mechanism—to SpMV to fuse preprocessing and per-row computation on the GPU, eliminating host interaction and improving cache locality.

mx.speedup: up to 7.19x (mean 3.35x, SD 1.89) over rocSPARSE LRB for single SpMV; beats rocSPARSE CSR-Adaptive for up to 92 consecutive SpMV calls
mx.other: 75% reduction in code complexity; fixed 25 MiB data structure vs. matrix-size-scaling rocSPARSE LRB structures

th: device-driven GPU self-scheduling for sparse matrix-vector multiplication

t: SpecEE: Accelerating Large Language Model Inference with Speculative Early Exiting
pb: Early exiting for LLM inference is bottlenecked by the predictor, which must search over a vocabulary of ~30,000 tokens per layer and incurs up to 20% overall inference latency overhead. Existing predictors also fail to integrate with speculative decoding token trees without exponential mapping complexity.
me: SpecEE introduces a speculative-model-based paradigm that uses a small draft model to reduce the token vocabulary search space for the early-exit predictor. It redesigns the predictor to exploit inherent data variation and GPU parallelism to cut computational complexity, uses layer-wise activation frequency profiling to weight predictor deployment non-uniformly across layers, and develops a tree-aware mapping that handles the full speculative decoding token tree without exponential blowup.
nv: Using a speculative draft model to shrink the predictor's runtime search space so that early exiting and speculative decoding compose efficiently.

mx.other: predictor overhead reduced from ~20% to lower; specific end-to-end speedup not stated in abstract

th: speculative early exiting for LLM inference

t: Insights into DeepSeek-V3: Scaling Challenges and Reflections on Hardware for AI Architectures
pb: Training and serving 671B-parameter MoE LLMs at scale exposes critical hardware bottlenecks: HBM memory capacity growing <50%/year versus >1000%/year model memory demand, FP8 Tensor Core accumulation precision limited to 13 mantissa bits (FP22) causing numerical instability in large-scale training, NVLink bandwidth halved in H800 vs H100 (400 vs 900 GB/s) constraining tensor parallelism, and all-to-all expert parallelism (EP) communication consuming up to 20 GPU SMs for control-plane operations.
me: The paper presents DeepSeek-V3's production architecture and infrastructure as a case study, covering: (1) Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) that compresses KV cache from 516 KB/token (LLaMA-3.1-405B) to 70 KB/token via low-rank KV projection; (2) DeepSeekMoE with Node-Limited Routing constraining expert token dispatch to at most 4 of 8 nodes to exploit the 4:1 NVLink/IB bandwidth ratio, reducing inter-node IB traffic; (3) FP8 mixed-precision training with tile-wise 1x128 activation quantization and block-wise 128x128 weight quantization using DeepGEMM, requiring workarounds for FP22 accumulation precision on Hopper; (4) DualPipe overlapping MLA and MoE computation with all-to-all EP dispatch/combine via InfiniBand GPUDirect Async (IBGDA); (5) a Multi-Plane Two-Layer Fat-Tree (MPFT) network replacing a standard three-layer fat-tree, using 8 independent IB planes per node to support up to 16,384 GPUs at the same cost-per-endpoint as a two-layer topology. Experimental data includes real cluster training throughput (272.8B tokens/day, MFU 43.7%), EP bandwidth (>40 GB/s per GPU), and network latency comparisons (IB at 2.8 us same-leaf vs RoCE at 3.6 us).
nv: Systematic hardware-software co-design analysis from a production 671B MoE LLM system that quantifies the bottlenecks in FP8 accumulation precision, NVLink/IB bandwidth asymmetry, and EP control-plane SM consumption, and proposes the Multi-Plane Fat-Tree topology as a cost-equivalent path to 8x scale-out beyond single-plane two-layer fat trees.

mx.speedup: MTP module achieves 1.8x generation TPS vs. no MTP; EP dispatch/combine >40 GB/s per GPU on MPFT; TPOT theoretical upper bound 67 tokens/s on H800 IB vs ~1200 tokens/s on GB200 NVL72
mx.energy_or_tops_w: MFU 43.73% (non-causal) on 2048 H800 GPUs; 250 GFLOPS/token for 671B MoE vs 2448 for LLaMA-405B dense
mx.accuracy: FP8 training relative accuracy loss <0.25% vs BF16
mx.other: KV cache: 70 KB/token (MLA) vs 516 KB/token (LLaMA-405B GQA); training throughput 272.8B tokens/day; 2,048 H800 GPUs for full DeepSeek-V3 training

th: Hardware-software co-design analysis of a production 671B MoE LLM system with hardware architecture recommendations

t: MEGA.mini: A Universal Generative AI Processor with a New Big/Little Core Architecture for NPU
pb: Generative AI processors must efficiently accelerate both non-diffusion models (VAEs, GANs, transformers) and diffusion models; diffusion models require 25–100x more operations due to iterative inference, creating a computational mismatch for single-architecture designs.
me: MEGA.mini implements a big/little core architecture where big cores optimize for NDM inference (CNNs, transformers) and little cores handle diffusion model iterative steps; heterogeneous compute fabric scales performance and energy across workload diversity.
nv: Big/little heterogeneous core architecture for NPUs differentiating between computationally-sparse NDMs and iterative-heavy diffusion models.
th: Heterogeneous big/little NPU for unified generative AI (NDM + diffusion) processing

t: 21.5 A Fully Integrated Multi-Phase Voltage Regulator with Enhanced Light-Load-Efficiency Peak of 86%, Featuring an Autonomous Mode Transition from Hard-Switching to Soft-Switching to Discontinuous Conduction Mode in 3nm FinFET CMOS
pb: Fully integrated voltage regulators (FIVRs) face efficiency challenges across the power spectrum: high efficiency at peak power (current surges) but poor efficiency at idle loads; soft-switching and DCM modes reduce ripple but degrade efficiency under high load.
me: 3nm FIVR with autonomous mode transition from hard-switching (high load) to soft-switching to discontinuous conduction mode (DCM) at light load, maintaining droop response while achieving 86% peak light-load efficiency.
nv: Autonomous multi-mode transition (hard-switching → soft-switching → DCM) optimizing efficiency across full load range.
th: Multi-mode FIVR optimizing full-spectrum load efficiency

t: 16.2 RNGD: A 5nm Tensor-Contraction Processor for Power-Efficient Inference on Large Language Models
pb: LLM inference accelerators face a challenge: traditional matrix-multiplication-based architectures fail to fully exploit parallelism and data locality inherent in tensor contractions, limiting throughput and efficiency for LLM workloads.
me: RNGD uses tensor contraction as the primitive computational unit instead of matrix multiplication, enabling massive parallelism and time-axis pipelining similar to vector processors; processing elements can be dynamically split into smaller slices with configurable fetch networks for flexible parallelism.

t: Dissecting and Modeling the Architecture of Modern GPU Cores

All findings are integrated into a rebuilt Accel-sim model validated against real hardware.
